[Problem]{.card-kicker} **Number of Good Pairs** [LC 1512 · Number of Good Pairs](https://leetcode.com/problems/number-of-good-pairs/){difficulty="Easy"}

This is the smallest possible member of the pair-counting family, and worth taking slowly because every harder problem in @sec-cnt-p2 reuses its shape. A "pair" here is an **index pair with a value condition**, not a subarray: nothing is contiguous, and the only thing that matters is which values sit where.

The first swap is to stop enumerating pairs. Read the definition from the point of view of the **right endpoint**: when the right end is $j$, any earlier slot $i$ holding the same value makes a good pair, so the number of pairs that end at $j$ is exactly "how many times have I already seen `nums[j]`". One hash table (or, since $1 \le nums[i] \le 100$, a 101-slot direct-address array) carrying those counts turns the double loop into a single pass: `ans += seen[v]; seen[v] += 1`. For `[1,2,3,1,1,3]` the per-slot counts are $0,0,0,1,2,1$, which add up to $4$ — the sample.

The second swap is the contribution technique of @sec-cnt-a1 applied to pairs instead of windows. The condition $nums[i] == nums[j]$ cares only about the **value**, so group the indices by value: a value seen $c$ times contributes every unordered pair drawn from its $c$ positions, i.e. $\binom{c}{2} = c(c-1)/2$. For the sample the counts are $\{1:3,\; 2:1,\; 3:2\}$ and $\binom{3}{2} + \binom{1}{2} + \binom{2}{2} = 3 + 0 + 1 = 4$.

Both rungs are $O(n)$ and both are "the same sum, re-indexed": the one-pass tally charges each pair to its **right endpoint**, the histogram charges it to its **value**. The identity $\sum_j \text{seen}_j = \sum_v \binom{c_v}{2}$ is the reason they always agree, and it is the bookkeeping you should be able to reproduce under interview pressure — the third view (below) uses it to keep a running total without a second pass.
